title: Prescribing far from the norm for the same kind of prescriber
question: Which San Francisco prescribers write a far larger share of opioids or brand-name drugs, or far costlier prescriptions, than others of their kind in the same Medicare file?
finding: Of 6,413 San Francisco prescribers in the 2024 Medicare drug file, 26 stand far above their kind on the share of claims that are opioids, 42 on the share that are brand-name, and 32 wrote $2 million or more at ten times their kind's cost per claim. Highest opioid share: Adam Lee, PHARM.D. (provider no. 1467544031), pharmacist, 91% of 3,007 claims (kind's middle 0.0%). 6 of the opioid outliers give one street address, 3838 California St. Highest brand share: Sharrie Ray, M.D. (provider no. 1689751372), 98% of 22,833 claims, most often Shingrix (8,099 claims). Highest cost: Dong Phuong Nguyen, PHARMD (provider no. 1780776443), $15.3 million, most of it Biktarvy ($6.0 million).
how: From the federal Part D file by prescriber for 2024 (San Francisco addresses). Each prescriber is set against the middle and the top tenth of prescribers of the same federal type with 100 or more claims (types with 20 or more such prescribers). Opioid outlier: 200 or more claims, 100 or more opioid claims, and an opioid share at least three times the type's middle, in its top tenth and at least 20%. Brand outlier: 500 or more claims and a brand-name share at least twice the middle, in the top tenth and at least 30%. Cost outlier: $2 million or more and ten times the type's middle cost per claim. Opioid, long-acting opioid and brand counts are the file's own. The top drugs come from the companion file by prescriber and drug. "Physicians at the same address" is the most common physician type among other prescribers at the street address.
limits: The federal type is coarse: a physician assistant in an orthopedic-surgery office, a nurse practitioner in a palliative-care or cancer-pain service, and a pharmacist in a pain clinic would each be compared with every physician assistant, nurse practitioner or pharmacist, so the address column matters more than the rank. A specialist who prescribes a handful of very costly drugs will stand far above the type's cost per claim, and a high brand share can mean vaccines or newer drugs sold only under a brand; the files do not say what a drug treats, so each row names the costliest and the most-prescribed drug for the reader to check. The file does not mark which brand-name drugs have a generic equivalent, nor which drugs are often resold; neither test could be run from the files on disk. Claims are prescriptions filled, counted under the prescriber named on them; refills and prescriptions for nursing-home residents add up fast. Nothing here measures whether a prescription was appropriate.
